If a bottle filling up sound gets higher as the bottle gets filled, why does the sound of tapping the bottle get lower as the bottle gets filled?

I think the filling sound is from air vibrations above the liquid while tapping the bottle vibrates the bottle walls (dampened by the liquid).

If you think of a vibrating string within the volume of air as it shrinks, the string length gets shorter as the bottle fills and the air volume decreases. Shorter string = higher vibration frequency. Similarly, a string vibrating along the bottle walls within the liquid can get longer as the bottle fills. Longer string = lower frequency.

This is pretty much right. It's a question of resonant chambers. All matter when exposed to a physical shock will vibrate at its resonant frequency. This frequency is determined by several factors, but in general terms as size increases the resonant frequency decreases. Air (or any fluid) when contained in a chamber acts as a unified whole while vibrating. This resonant chamber decreases in size as the glass is filled, increasing the frequency of resonant vibration. Now the sound of water being poured is similar to white noise, or a broad spectrum of oscillations, but the chamber amplifies the vibrations at its ever increasing resonant point. When the bottle filled and tapped, the water is now the primary resonator, which pushes along the sides of the bottle from which the sound radiates. More water = more massive resonator = lower frequency.

All matter when exposed to a physical shock will vibrate at its resonant frequency.

Not exactly. Resonant frequency is a system property which varies by material and construction. When a system is vibrated by an external load at the resonant frequency, then the system magnifies the input energy. Resonance can be mitigated by various techniques to allow the system to dissipate energy. A system, to reach resonance, has to be excited at the system's resonant frequency. There are plenty of situations where a vibrating load on a system excites the system but does not cause the system to reach resonance.

While what you say is true, it's not exactly what I was describing. I was talking about how a system responds to an impulse of kinetic energy, not a sustained oscillatory input. In these situations the system will ring at its resonant frequency and fade out, instead of growing. Resonance can be technologically dampened, but almost everything naturally resonates to a greater or lesser degree.
Transient harmonic inputs can hit the resonance frequency of a system as well. It is a major concern in seismic engineering.
